newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Kashmir group proposes truce, demilitarisation.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir group proposes truce, demilitarisation.

text.p: A militant group fighting Indian rule in Kashmir on Monday proposed a truce and demilitarisation in the divided Himalayan region before setting up a U.N.-supervised transitional administration there.

The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) said in a statement its Pakistan-based chairman Amanullah Khan had written to the prime ministers of India and Pakistan calling for a democratic decision about Kashmir's future after five years' transitional government.
The JKLF is one of several Moslem militant groups fighting Indian rule over two-thirds of Kashmir, the remaining third of which is controlled by Pakistan.

Amanullah's identical letters to prime ministers Inder Kumar Gujral of India and Nawaz Sharif of Pakistan suggested that all pro-Pakistan, pro-India and pro-independence militants should agree to a ceasefire on a mutually agreed date, the JKLF statement said.

"Following the ceasefire, all armed forces and civil personnel of India and Pakistan (should) be withdrawn from the state and all militants disarmed -- all the three steps to be taken simultaneously and under U.N. supervision," it said.

"This should be followed by a reunification of the divided Jammu and Kashmir state and an interim administration formed under U.N. supervision, which should be turned gradually into a representative one by inducting into it notables from all regions, religions and different schools of political thought."

It said that after five years of transitional government, Kashmiris must decide "through democratic means" under U.N. supervision whether the region become an independent entity or form part of India or Pakistan.

New Delhi regards the whole of the region as an integral part of the Indian union. Islambad wants the predominantly Moslem Kashmiris to decide in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.

Some militant groups, such as the JKLF, want to reunite Kashmir into an independent state, an idea opposed by both India and Pakistan, which have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947 over Kashmir.
Gujral, on his first visit to Kashmir since assuming office last week, said on Sunday he had no plans to start talks with a leading organisation of Kashmiri separatists.
He is due to meet Sharif on the fringes of a summit of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation in the Maldives in May.
